generations.description: The original Camaro, Ford Mustang's competitor. Featured V8 engines and iconic styling. SS and Z/28 variants established Camaro as a performance car.
Larger second generation with improved styling. Featured big-block V8 engines. Z/28 and SS variants were high-performance models. Iconic in muscle car culture.
Smaller, more efficient Camaro. Featured V6 and V8 engines. IROC-Z variant became popular. Improved handling and fuel economy during fuel crisis era.
Final F-body Camaro. Featured LS1 V8 engine producing 305-320 horsepower. SS and Z28 variants were high-performance. Last generation before hiatus.
Camaro revival with retro-modern design. Featured V6 and V8 engines. SS and ZL1 variants offered high performance. Z/28 was track-focused model.
Alpha platform with improved handling. Featured updated V8 engines and improved technology. ZL1 with supercharged V8 produced 650 horsepower. 1LE track packages available.
Stingray design with iconic styling. Featured big-block and small-block V8 engines. Performance declined during fuel crisis but maintained Corvette's status as America's sports car.
Modern Corvette with improved technology. Featured updated V8 engines and improved handling. ZR-1 variant with DOHC V8 was a technological showcase.
Complete redesign with LS1 V8 engine. Featured improved handling and performance. Z06 variant was track-focused. Established modern Corvette performance.
Refined design with LS2/LS3 V8 engines. Z06 and ZR1 variants were high-performance. ZR1 with supercharged V8 produced 638 horsepower. Excellent value for performance.
Final front-engine Corvette. Featured LT1/LT4 V8 engines. Z06 and ZR1 variants were track-focused. ZR1 produced 755 horsepower. Advanced technology and aerodynamics.
First mid-engine Corvette. Featured LT2 V8 engine producing 490-495 horsepower. Z06 variant with flat-plane crank V8. Revolutionary design maintaining Corvette's performance legacy.

Modern performance sedan based on Holden Commodore VF. Featured 6.2L LS3 V8 engine producing 415 horsepower. Rear-wheel drive with excellent handling. Popular among enthusiasts for modification potential and sleeper appeal.

Original Chevelle SS, initially as Malibu SS trim. Rare Z16 option introduced 396 big-block V8 in 1965. SS 396 became dedicated performance series from 1966-67. Established Chevelle as a muscle car icon.
Redesigned body style with SS as performance option/package. Peak performance in 1970 with SS 454 LS6 engine rated at ~450 gross horsepower. Iconic muscle car generation with big-block V8 engines.
Colonnade body style. SS badge offered as appearance and performance package on Malibu models. Power reduced due to emissions regulations and safety standards. Last year of true Chevelle SS.
Known as Chevy II with Nova designation. SS badge introduced in 1963 as trim/package on Nova 400 Sport Coupe and Convertible. Lightweight compact muscle car foundation.
Continued as Chevy II/Nova SS with styling revisions. SS remained performance-appearance package. Popular among enthusiasts for compact size and V8 power.

Nova name solidified. SS became its own series (1968-70) then reverted to option package. Engine power peaked early; SS identity shifted toward appearance in later years. Classic 'pocket rocket' muscle car.
Final Nova SS years. Performance edge lost due to emissions; emphasis shifted to appearance/luxury trims. SS discontinued after 1976. Last of the classic Nova SS models.
A-body El Camino based on Chevelle platform. SS-396 introduced as separate model in 1968. Peak SS performance in 1970 with LS6 454 engine. Unique muscle car/pickup hybrid design.

Colonnade body style. SS offered primarily as trim/option level. Less potent than earlier SS big-block models due to stricter emissions and safety regulations. More cosmetic and handling features than pure performance.

G-body downsized generation. SS returned as full trim and appearance package. By mid-1980s, SS often carried 5.0L V8, though power was much lower than earlier SS models. Final generation of El Camino.

First Cobalt SS with 2.0L LSJ Ecotec supercharged engine producing ~205 horsepower. Available only as coupe. Popular among tuners for lightweight design and modification potential. Discontinued due to emissions regulations.

Relaunched with 2.0L LNF Ecotec turbocharged engine producing ~260 horsepower and 260 lb-ft torque. Available as coupe (2008-2010) and sedan (2009 only). Featured Reconfigurable Performance Display. Highly tunable compact performance car.
First Monte Carlo SS package offered. Featured Turbo-Jet 454 big-block V8 engines. Luxury-muscle blend with emphasis on styling, suspension, and comfort as well as power.
SS reintroduced after hiatus. Featured smaller V8 engines and sporty owner trims. Special 'Aerocoupe' versions in 1986-87. Emphasized styling, suspension, and comfort alongside performance.
SS version revived for final Monte Carlo generation. Engines evolved from V6 to supercharged V6 to late 5.3L V8. Personal luxury coupe with performance focus. Final generation of Monte Carlo.

Impala SS reintroduced on rear-wheel-drive B-body platform with LT1 5.7L V8 producing 260-305 horsepower. SS was the only Impala version offered. Modern interpretation of classic full-size performance sedan.

Impala SS on front-wheel-drive W-body platform. 2004-2005 featured supercharged 3.8L V6 (L67). 2006-2009 upgraded to 5.3L V8 (LS4) with Active Fuel Management. Full-size performance sedan with modern technology.

Performance SUV variant with LS2 6.0L V8 producing ~395 horsepower and 400 lb-ft torque. Fast for its class with V8 power in SUV chassis. Rare example of SS badge on large SUV. Popular among truck/SUV enthusiasts.
4.8/5.3/6.0L LS-based V8s. Silverado SS 2003-2006, 6.0L 345 hp.
K2XX platform. 4.3L V6, 5.3L L83, 6.2L L86 EcoTec3 V8s.
T1 platform. 2.7L I4T, 5.3L L84, 6.2L L87, 3.0L Duramax. ZR2.
4.8/5.3L V8 full-size SUV.
K2XX. 5.3L L83 / 6.2L L86 V8s. RST variant.
T1 with IRS. 5.3L L84 / 6.2L L87 / 3.0L Duramax.
Long-WB GMT800. 5.3/6.0/8.1L V8s.
